content: Sudan staining involves the application of Sudan dyes to selectively stain substances that are sudanophilic, primarily lipids. The specific dyes used in this process include Sudan II, Sudan III, Sudan IV, Oil Red O, and Sudan Black B. These dyes exhibit a strong affinity for fats, making them particularly useful for identifying triglycerides, lipids, and lipoproteins. Typically, alcoholic solutions of Sudan dyes are employed for staining, although pyridine solutions may be utilized in certain circumstances. One common application of the Sudan stain test is to measure fecal fat levels, which aids in diagnosing steatorrhea. To perform the test, a small sample is dissolved in water or saline. Glacial acetic acid is then added to hydrolyze any insoluble fatty acid salts. Following this, a few drops of an alcoholic solution of Sudan III are introduced. The sample is subsequently spread onto a microscopic slide and heated twice to the boiling point. Under normal conditions, a stool sample should reveal only a few red-orange stained fat droplets when observed under a microscope. While this method is only semi-quantitative, its simplicity makes it a valuable tool for initial screening purposes.
